name: Tazarotene
summary: The strongest topical retinoid — reserved for patients who have plateaued on tretinoin or adapalene and can tolerate more irritation for more effect.
good: Retinoid-experienced patients with residual comedonal or inflammatory acne who need more potency than adapalene or tretinoin provided.
bad: Pregnancy — tazarotene carries a stricter contraindication than tretinoin/adapalene; also avoid stacking with physical scrubs or high-percentage acids, especially early on.
clinicalPearls: Short-contact therapy exists specifically because tazarotene’s irritation, not its efficacy, is usually the limiting factor — controlling contact time is a legitimate way to keep the benefit while taming the downside.
mechanism: Prodrug converted to active tazarotenic acid; RAR-β/γ selective with the strongest comedolytic and anti-inflammatory effect of the topical retinoids.
originalFields: Prodrug converted to active tazarotenic acid; RAR-β/γ selective with the strongest comedolytic and anti-inflammatory effect of the topical retinoids.
More severe or refractory comedonal-inflammatory acne, or patients who have built tolerance to gentler retinoids.
Can outpace tretinoin/adapalene, but at the cost of more pronounced irritation along the way.
Highest of the three retinoids — significant erythema and peeling are common, especially in the first weeks.
Effective for PIH via the same turnover mechanism, but the higher irritation burden carries proportionally higher risk of irritant-triggered pigmentation in darker skin if not carefully titrated.
The most pronounced barrier disruption among topical retinoids.
Leave-on, though "short-contact" application — applying and washing off after a set time, gradually extended — is a specific strategy used to reduce irritation while keeping benefit.
Usually introduced only after a patient has already built retinoid tolerance on tretinoin or adapalene, rather than as a first retinoid.
